target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers for most voters
objection: A federal holiday would not guarantee paid time off from private employers, so many low-wage workers—especially in retail, food service, health support, and gig work—would still have to work and face the same voting barrier under a holiday in name only. The policy would also create inequity because workers whose employers already offer time off would benefit while those who most need flexibility might not.

target: AG1's implication that a national holiday is the best primary solution to the voting-access problem
objection: Instead of relying on a symbolic holiday, the more reliable approach is to change voting logistics directly—such as requiring employers to provide time for voting, or using automatic voter registration and simpler ID/registration rules—because research and prior experience suggest an election-day holiday by itself is usually less effective than targeted access reforms.

target: AG2's assumption that a holiday would be purely symbolic and leave workers exposed
objection: A national holiday is intended to create a broad default of closed schools and reduced work scheduling, so most people are not forced to choose between voting and earning wages; it can also be paired with paid leave or other time-to-vote protections, meaning it does not have to be merely symbolic.

target: AG1's revised claim that a holiday plus extra protections would solve the problem
objection: If a holiday needs to be paired with workplace protections to work, then the holiday itself is redundant or politically distracting, because federal holiday status alone still does not guarantee paid time off for private workers and many retail/service jobs will remain open.

target: AG1's comparison of Election Day holidays to other OECD countries
objection: The international comparison is not apples-to-apples, because countries that hold elections on holidays often also have broader labor protections or different paid-leave systems. In the U.S., without enforceable employer-time mandates, low-income hourly workers may benefit least and inequality could worsen.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday must be the only policy change to matter
objection: The holiday is not meant to stand alone; it is a structural step that changes the baseline calendar for schools and many public institutions, reducing the need for people to scramble for time off and making voting easier in combination with other rules.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is redundant if workplace protections are also needed
objection: A nationwide holiday creates coordination effects—schools close, workplaces often reduce hours or shut down, and election administrators can plan more predictably—so it lowers default scheduling conflict and lost-wage costs even before other protections are added.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday creates useful coordination effects
objection: Concentrating voting into a single holiday can create peak demand and longer lines, which harms inflexible workers who cannot wait or return multiple times. Spreading access through early voting, vote-by-mail, and streamlined registration is less burdensome because it distributes demand over time instead of moving everyone to the same day.

target: AG2's concern that a holiday will create long lines and peak demand
objection: A holiday does not force everyone to vote at the same moment; by removing work and school conflicts, it allows people to vote over a wider range of hours throughout the day, and election administrators can plan for more staffing and capacity because the date is fixed and predictable.

target: AG1's claim that reduced work/school conflict is enough to solve the barrier
objection: The central problem for many low-income workers is not just timing but income security and employer control; they may still be scheduled or lose wages unless there are enforceable, targeted time-to-vote or paid-leave rules. If those protections are needed anyway, the holiday becomes unnecessary as the centerpiece policy and could weaken enforcement or distract from the real fix.

target: AG2's focus on paid leave as the main concern
objection: A national holiday changes the baseline calendar for schools and many public institutions, reducing the number of people who need to ask or negotiate for time off and making it easier for workplaces and communities to coordinate around voting.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday causes peak congestion
objection: Election Day on a holiday does not force voting into one narrow window; instead it removes the after-work and before-school rush, and jurisdictions can plan staffing and polling capacity around the fixed day more effectively.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday improves overall accessibility and logistics
objection: The holiday still mainly affects calendar convenience, while low-income workers' biggest problem is employer control and lost income. If the real goal is reliable access, targeted reforms like voting-time rules or registration/ID simplification are more direct and do not depend on school closures or on employers honoring the holiday in practice.

target: AG1's suggestion that school/public-facility coordination makes a holiday useful for voting
objection: Election administration logistics are separate from workers' ability to vote; polling-site capacity can be improved directly by funding staffing, contracts, and access arrangements, without turning Election Day into a holiday that still leaves many hourly workers without paid time off or protection from wage loss.

target: AG2's framing of Election Day as only a paid-time-off issue
objection: A national holiday changes the broader social environment for the day: schools are out, communities can organize transportation and childcare support, and voting becomes a shared civic activity rather than an individual scramble, which can make participation easier for families.

target: AG1's claim that civic-event framing naturally makes voting fit normal family routines
objection: For low-income families, school closures can create new burdens such as paid childcare or supervision gaps, while hourly service and essential workers still face employer-controlled schedules and possible wage loss. So the holiday may simply shift the burden from finding time to vote to finding coverage for the day, and without enforced time-to-vote rules it may widen rather than reduce inequality.

target: AG2's argument that workers still need paid leave and that the holiday is therefore ineffective
objection: A national holiday also improves system capacity by making more people available to serve as poll workers and by helping election administrators open and staff polling sites. That can increase locations, poll-site hours, and reduce congestion even if not every employer provides paid leave.
